The Southern shortfin squid (Illex coindetii) displays a pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, with females attaining a mantle length at death of 35.0 centimeters [Li = 35.0 centimeters], while males are considerably smaller at 32.0 centimeters [Li = 32.0 centimeters] when they succumb to senescent mortality. This size disparity is characteristic of many ommastrephid squids and is linked to the higher energetic demands of female gamete production. Data from field-collected specimens indicate that the onset of puberty in females occurs at a mantle length of 14.0 centimeters [Lp = 14.0 centimeters], a size at which the microscopic processes of gametogenesis first become detectable in histological sections. Males, in contrast, initiate gonadal development at a smaller body size, reaching puberty at a mantle length of 10.0 centimeters [Lp = 10.0 centimeters]. This earlier maturation in males is a widespread pattern among cephalopods and likely reflects a strategy to maximize reproductive opportunities in a short-lived, semelparous life cycle.

At a constant water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the embryonic development of Illex coindetii proceeds rapidly, culminating in hatching after an incubation period of approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days]. These newly hatched paralarvae are minuscule, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a mass that reflects the small size of the fertilized egg from which they emerge. The exotrophic transition occurs almost immediately, as the yolk reserves are exhausted within hours of hatching, compelling the young paralarvae to commence active feeding on small zooplankton. The thermal dependence of early ontogeny is pronounced; under cooler conditions the incubation period would lengthen considerably, underscoring the role of temperature in determining the timing of recruitment pulses in this commercially important species.

Under the same stable thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], male Southern shortfin squid exhibit a shorter lifespan than females, although the maximum documented longevity for females reaches 365 days [am = 365 days]. This annual lifespan places Illex coindetii among the shorter-lived ommastrephids, a life-history strategy that necessitates a single, massive reproductive effort at the end of life. Females channel the entirety of their accumulated somatic reserves into a single batch of eggs, resulting in a cumulative reproductive output at death of 800,000 eggs  when reared at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This high fecundity compensates for the absence of parental care and the high mortality rates experienced during the planktonic larval phase.

The physiological cost of this semelparous reproductive strategy is starkly illustrated by the post-spawning mortality observed in both sexes. After the single spawning event, females and males alike undergo a rapid and irreversible physiological deterioration, a process that has been linked to the failure of homeostatic regulation following the exhaustive allocation of resources to gamete production. The mantle length at death for females, 35.0 centimeters [Li = 35.0 centimeters], represents the culmination of a growth trajectory that prioritizes somatic expansion during the juvenile phase before a final, explosive investment in reproduction. In males, the corresponding value of 32.0 centimeters [Li = 32.0 centimeters] is attained more quickly, allowing them to mature and mate before the females of their cohort reach their terminal size.

Comparative studies within the genus Illex reveal that the age at birth of 12 days [ab = 12 days] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] is typical for the group, though local adaptation to thermal regimes can shift this value by several days. The wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] is similarly consistent with the small egg diameters reported for the genus. The onset of puberty in females occurs at a mantle length of 14.0 centimeters [Lp = 14.0 centimeters], a value that is roughly 40 percent of the terminal mantle length and aligns with the general ommastrephid pattern of initiating reproduction only after a substantial fraction of the growth potential has been realized. For males, the pubertal mantle length of 10.0 centimeters [Lp = 10.0 centimeters] is proportionally smaller, reinforcing the interpretation that male reproductive maturity is decoupled from the attainment of near-maximal body size.
